highlights.titleZh: Anthropic’s IPO shows AI’s value, but enterprises should stay wary | TechTarget
highlights.content: Anthropic today became the first AI model maker to go public, just a week shy of the fourth anniversary of the launch of its archrival OpenAI’s pioneering ChatGPT, bolstering the value of AI for enterprises that are still struggling with the ROI of the technology and overshadowing AI competitors. The historic public offering from the creator of the Claude line of generative AI models started at $110.50, 34% above the IPO price set on Wednesday. It raised about $81.3 billion across 980 million shares, shattering SpaceX's previous $75 billion record. With the vendor's first day trading on the public market - under the stock ticker symbol ANT - exceeding expectations, it also provided some assurance across the AI industry that financial value lies in the technology, even as enterprises are still scurrying to demonstrate ROI in how they have incorporated it. "The fact they got way above the offering price should give enterprises confidence that enterprise AI is a real thing," said Nick Patience, an analyst at Futurum Group. "For CIOs in some ways it lowers the risk of betting on the company." The dramatic public offering comes after Anthropic initially predicted its valuation would be about $1.33 trillion. The actual value ended up at $1.5 trillion. That initial devaluation in early November followed the Nov. 3 mid-term elections, which revealed widespread negative sentiment in the U.S. about AI and AI data centers. It also comes amid an AI market grappling with the reality of expensive technology that has mostly yet to yield a return. The lack of immediate ROI has led AI vendors, including Anthropic, to try to pacify enterprise concerns by cutting prices. Not only did Anthropic’s first day being listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange give some measure of certainty to enterprises, but it also provided even more visibility to vendor’s technology. ### **What the new funding means** The generative AI startup has spent the six years since it was founded focusing on the enterprise market, compared to OpenAI, which has only lately made serious inroads with businesses. So, the record-breaking IPO suggests that Anthropic’s approach is correct. Its successful debut as a public company means it can now continue to purchase compute and raise debt easily. "Anthropic was already sitting on more than $100 billion before the IPO," Patience noted. "The new money buys it use over its supply chains." He added that Anthropic can now step into some of the deals that before appeared uncertain, using prepayments or guarantees to secure capacity. "Over time, it could own more of its infrastructure outright," Patience continued. He was referring to the fact that currently Anthropic mostly holds contracts in which it rents compute and cloud services from vendors such as AWS, Google Cloud and Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Now, with access to more capital, the vendor could one day buy instead of lease the compute it needs. However, going public also means Anthropic needs to slow down its participation in the price war, he said. Along with OpenAI and others, the vendor has been lowering the prices of its models to compete with models from open-weight vendors - most of them from China - whose models are on par with some frontier models. "They will continue to cut those prices, Patience said. “I wonder if they will cut them maybe at a slightly slower rate than they were going to because Wall Street will put a new kind of pressure on the company that they've never had before," Other than using its new $81.3 billion cash storehouse to buy compute power, the AI vendor will also be encouraged to create more advanced models and other new technology and products that build on AI, said Michael Bennett, associate vice chancellor for data science and AI strategy. highlights.content: Ever wonder how artificial intelligence develops enhanced capabilities? Look no further than frontier AI labs. These startups operate at the cutting edge of the AI industry, driving breakthroughs like foundation models and multi-agent systems, while enforcing safety and alignment standards to ensure the technology supports the common good. As a result, AI has gone from fringe invention to mainstream tool. ## Top Frontier AI Labs - Anthropic - OpenAI - SpaceXSI - Google DeepMind - Meta The global AI market is expected to reach nearly $2 trillion by 2032, according to a 2026 Statista report, with several tech titans primed to go public in the near future — including a few frontier labs on this list. Here are some of the top frontier AI lab companies pushing the limits of artificial intelligence and writing the next chapter of the AI narrative. ## Frontier AI Labs to Know Formerly xAI, SpaceXSI creates AI models for image and voice generation, as well as bot assistants. Its best-known application, though, is running the Grok chatbot, which compiles real-time data from the X platform to inform its responses to user queries. SpaceXSI trains its AI systems using Colossus, one of the world’s largest supercomputers that the company built in just over four months. DeepSeek is the Chinese startup behind DeepSeek-R1, which sent shockwaves through the tech world after rivaling the performance of its larger American counterparts at a fraction of the size and cost. The company has doubled down on this trend with its V4-Flash and V4.1-Flash releases, delivering competitive capabilities in even smaller models and changing the economics of AI as companies look to cut costs. Google DeepMind brings together machine learning experts, scientists and engineers to extend the reasoning abilities of AI. The lab’s Gemini 4 Argon model demonstrates long-horizon reasoning for tasks in areas like cybersecurity and software engineering, and it supports products like Google’s Gemini app and AI mode in search. DeepMind then released Gemini 4 Carbon shortly after, continuing to increase its models’ reasoning capacity. Thinking Machines Lab is an startup founded by Mira Murati, former chief technology officer at OpenAI. The lab aims to promote a collaborative approach by consistently sharing its research and parameters and developing models that rely on human intervention to function. Its first AI model, Inkling, is intended as a “generalist” model with a well-rounded skill set that covers coding, reasoning and agentic tool use. Anthropic is an AI startup best known for its Claude chatbot, including an enterprise version that excels at coding. The company has a reputation for prioritizing AI safety, as demonstrated by its delayed release of its powerful Claude Mythos model. It also has a frontier team dedicated to understanding AI systems and developing best practices. More recently, the team has researched methods to prove that outputs come from a specific AI model. Meta is an AI and virtual reality company committed to designing AI for everyday individual use under its “personal superintelligence” vision. Behind the scenes, the company reorganized its AI initiatives under Meta Superintelligence Labs to accelerate its research. The lab has hit the ground running, releasing the compact Muse Spark model and a “personal AI agent” called Meta Muse that completes multi-step tasks with little to no supervision. OpenAI ushered in the modern era of generative AI when it released its ChatGPT chatbot in 2022, bringing conversational AI to the masses. That said, the startup’s ultimate goal is to achieve artificial general intelligence, or AI that can think and learn as humans do. To that end, OpenAI has directed its research efforts toward designing multimodal models that can efficiently process written, visual and audio data. highlights.content: Scale launched Scale for Hospital Operations on November 16, 2026, introducing five model-agnostic, on-premises AI agents targeting the administrative and clinical workflows that create care backlogs in health systems \[1]. The suite directly addresses the two most-cited enterprise AI adoption barriers: agent reliability and hallucination management (55.4%) \[2] and data privacy and security vulnerabilities (52.6%) \[2]. Three proprietary benchmarks and a clinician-led evaluation framework anchor the launch, positioning Scale as a rigorous vertical AI vendor rather than a general-purpose platform \[1]. ## What is Covered in this Article - Five purpose-built hospital operations agents and their workflow targets \[1] - On-premises, model-agnostic architecture as a response to enterprise AI adoption barriers \[2] - Proprietary healthcare benchmarks establishing measurable reliability standards \[1] - Clinical evidence quantifying the burnout relief agentic AI can deliver \[1] - Scale's vertical AI portfolio strategy within a fast-growing AI platforms market \[3]\[1] **The News:** Scale announced Scale for Hospital Operations on November 16, 2026, comprising five agents built for the high-volume workflows that accumulate outside the exam room \[1]. The five applications are: Scheduling Intelligence, Order Guidance, Medical Record Review & Summarization, Safety & Incident Investigation, and Clinical Documentation & Quality Review \[1]. Each agent runs inside the health system's own environment, works with any model, and is deployed alongside Scale engineers and clinical subject-matter experts \[1]. Scale also published three proprietary healthcare benchmarks, CliniCARE-Bench, PSEBench, and DistressBench, to support pre-deployment reliability evaluation \[1]. The company described the launch as the first part of a broader and growing portfolio, with additional agents rolling out over coming months \[1]. ## Scale Moves Into Hospital Operations With Five Purpose-Built AI Agents **Analysis:** Scale's move into hospital operations is a deliberate vertical expansion, not a feature addition. By deploying agents inside health system environments with clinician-led evaluation, Scale is directly engineering around the two barriers most likely to stall enterprise AI programs: 55.4% of AI decision-makers cite agent reliability and hallucination management as a challenge \[2], and 52.6% cite data privacy and security vulnerabilities \[2]. The architecture is the answer to the objection before the objection is raised. ### Five Agents, One Coherent Workflow Strategy The five agents map precisely to the workflows where hospital backlogs form outside the exam room \[1]. The Scheduling Intelligence Agent triages referrals by clinical urgency and reworks existing schedules to accommodate urgent patients. The Order Guidance Agent flags missing tests and recommends labs, imaging, and prescriptions with cited evidence. The Medical Record Review & Summarization Agent assembles a patient's history with each finding linked to its source document \[1]. The Safety & Incident Investigation Agent surfaces recurring patterns in safety reports rather than processing them in arrival order. The Clinical Documentation & Quality Review Agent drafts reports for clinician sign-off and checks documentation against hospital guidelines \[1]. Together, the suite addresses two of the top enterprise GenAI use-case priorities: operations and workflow orchestration, cited by 51.1% of decision-makers \[2], and document analysis and summarization, cited by 51.7% \[2]. ### Architecture Built Around the Adoption Barriers The on-premises, model-agnostic deployment model is a direct structural response to the enterprise AI adoption market. highlights.content: Member-only story # 9 Free GitHub Repos That Make AI Tools Way More Powerful ## From smarter Claude workflows to better-looking websites and native Mac apps, these open-source projects are worth adding to your AI toolkit. Meanwhile, developers are building entire workflows around AI, using open-source projects that give these tools new capabilities. I went through nine interesting projects that take things a little further. Some help Claude catch mistakes before writing code, others improve website design and SEO, and a few let you build software that would normally require several different tools. Here are the ones worth checking out. ## 1. Elephant Goldfish: Make Claude Better at Planning One of the biggest limitations of AI coding tools is that they can confidently follow a flawed plan. Claude might suggest an approach, start building it, and only discover major problems much later. The issue is that asking the same AI to review its own work doesn't always catch everything.

The job description paints a picture of an AI system that goes far beyond Apple Intelligence's current parlor tricks. We're talking about an agent that can browse the web autonomously, orchestrate workflows across multiple apps, generate code, and call external services - all the hallmarks of the agentic AI systems that have become tech's hottest battleground in recent months.

LLMs.content: # “You’re right”—LLMs will get climate info wrong if you ask Some models fare better, but all fail in similar ways. Many studies over the years have examined how people encounter climate science information. Some focused on the top results that Google surfaced (back when Google was still in the business of serving links), while others examined social media content or newspaper and TV news coverage. With large language models (LLMs) now forming a share of the public information diet, it’s worth looking at how they handle climate change. But there’s no direct way for researchers to look at the information people have seen. It is served ephemerally to individual users, confined to their chat session. A study led by researchers from University College London and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) tried to tackle this question from multiple angles, testing LLMs with different prompts and evaluating their output. They started with benchmarks of simple factual questions (benchmarks that might even be in models’ training data at this point) but also analyzed more complex interactions—including when users think they’re right to push back on an answer. ## CO2 Q&A LLM research often faces (no-true-Scotsman-tinged) criticism for focusing on a particular model rather than some other frontier model that may have been released after the experiment concluded. In this case, the study used 33 models, including multiple versions of the major frontier and open-weight models. The flagship frontier models used were Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and GPT-5.6 Sol. (You can find the full list in the report.) All the models were scored for correct answers to 600 questions from several benchmark sets. This included multiple-choice textbook questions, “reading comprehension” questions based on text snippets from scientific papers, and questions about how confident climate scientists are in different conclusions drawn from IPCC reports. That last one was the most difficult, with the flagship models answering around 78 percent correctly and the smallest open-weight models coming in at around 47 percent. For the other benchmarks, frontier models and large open-weight models generally scored around 90 percent, while small open-weight models scored in the 70s. Two persistent trends show up here: The latest frontier models tend to score a bit better than earlier generations of that model, and larger open-weight models score better than small ones. (For example, the models were asked whether the statement that “renewable energy investment kills jobs” is accurate, given evidence like descriptions of employment and investment statistics.) Here, the best models scored around 70 percent accuracy, while the worst models scored below 40 percent. Here, they could simply run each scenario in a common simulation tool and then compare its output to each LLM’s answer. LLMs.titleZh: Falsification Framework Improves Scientific Agent Reasoning Across Four
LLMs.content: Computer scientists have introduced FalsifyAgent, a verification framework designed to audit conclusions produced by large language model scientific agents by subjecting them to backward abductive reconstruction and adversarial co-evolution. Reported in the Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences by Hui Xiao, Hongwei Wang, and Meng Wang, the system addresses structural vulnerabilities in standard confirmatory verification methods that solely seek positive evidence matches for forward reasoning chains. Conventional checking paradigms often fail to detect omitted logical dependencies, ignore mutually exclusive alternative hypotheses supported by the same evidence, and remain susceptible to criterion-aware generation where models produce formally verifiable yet substantively inaccurate statements. To counteract these limitations, the authors recast trustworthiness from a static binary pass or fail check into procedural survival against progressively stronger adversarial challenges, establishing an evaluation framework grounded in the philosophy of scientific falsification. The theoretical architecture of FalsifyAgent centers on the Adversarially Robust Credibility Score, which quantifies credibility as the continuous area under a conclusion’s survival curve across iterative generations of falsification testing. Under uniform positive conditional bounds on attack coverage and correct adjudication, the researchers proved a conditional decay bound showing that the expected score for an objectively false assertion diminishes toward zero as testing generations increase. Rather than assuming unattacked reasoning chains are dependable, the framework enforces three axiomatic principles: conclusions must explicitly define testable operational failure conditions to be admitted, credibility can only be accumulated by surviving structured challenges, and every adversarial challenge must carry verifiable evidence rather than speculative objections. These operational constraints ensure that both generative and verifying components remain bounded by concrete empirical facts, preventing indefinite stalling or trivial semantic evasion during multi-agent interactions. The operational workflow operates across three primary stages, shifting focus away from initial text generation to systematic adversarial auditing. In the first stage, user inquiries undergo intent normalization, retrieval-augmented generation, and automated entity-relation knowledge graph construction. During evidence ingestion, items receive attack-surface metadata annotations detailing their publication dates, evidential strength tiers, sample sizes, and whether they derive from uncorroborated single sources. Stage two generates candidate multi-step reasoning chains while applying lightweight online adversarial probing to each intermediate step immediately after generation. By rolling back and regenerating steps that fail elementary one-generation attack probes, the pipeline eliminates superficial errors before entering expensive verification loops. Prior to deep testing, an admission check extracts the core claim, scope, and operational failure boundaries, achieving an admission coverage of 98.3 percent on a dedicated 120-item development set. Stage three forms the core contribution through two tightly coupled mechanisms: backward abductive reconstruction and dynamic adversarial co-evolution. In backward reconstruction, the system works in reverse from the generated conclusion to build an evidence-demand tree, recursively identifying the minimal necessary premises required for the claim to hold. The demand tree explicitly distinguishes between must-exist requirements that demand verified positive evidence and must-not-exist requirements that require an active search for counterexamples. LLMs.titleZh: What Is An LLM? Large Language Models Explained
LLMs.content: # What Is an LLM? Large Language Models Explained **A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on large amounts of text to understand and generate human language. LLMs predict the most likely next piece of text, one token at a time, which lets them answer questions, write and summarize documents, generate code, and power AI agents that take actions.** For the short definition, see the LLM entry in Monte Carlo’s glossary. GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, and Mistral are all families of LLMs. They sit behind chatbots, coding assistants, enterprise search, and the growing number of AI agents companies are putting into production. This guide covers what an LLM is, how it works, what it’s good and bad at, and what it takes to trust one once real users depend on it. ## Key takeaways - An LLM is a type of AI model trained to predict text. Most modern LLMs use the transformer architecture. - LLMs are probabilistic: the same prompt can produce different answers. - Output quality depends heavily on the context the model receives at runtime, not just on the model itself. - An LLM generates text. An AI agent uses an LLM to plan and take actions, like calling tools and querying data. - In production, most LLM failures trace back to bad context, wrong tool use, or changes in the model or data, and they often fail silently. ## What does LLM stand for? LLM stands for **large language model**. - **Large** refers to the scale: billions of parameters (the internal numeric weights the model learns) trained on enormous text datasets. - **Language** refers to what it works with: words, sentences, code, and other text-like data. - **Model** means it’s a trained system that makes predictions. (See What is an AI model?) ## How do LLMs work? At its core, an LLM does one thing: given some text, it predicts what text should come next. Repeating that prediction many times produces sentences, paragraphs, and full answers. ### 1. Text becomes tokens LLMs don’t read words the way people do. They break text into tokens, which are roughly words or parts of words. “Unbelievable” might become “un,” “believ,” and “able.” Usage limits, context window size, and pricing are all measured in tokens. ### 2. Tokens become numbers Each token is converted into a vector, a list of numbers that captures something about its meaning and its relationship to other tokens. Similar ideas end up with similar vectors. (The same idea powers embeddings and vector databases.) ### 3. The transformer weighs context Most modern LLMs use the **transformer** architecture, introduced by Google researchers in the 2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need.” Its key mechanism, **attention**, lets the model weigh how much every token in the input matters to every other token. That’s how an LLM knows that “it” in “the server crashed because it ran out of memory” refers to the server. ### 4. The model predicts the next token The model outputs a probability for every possible next token, picks one (with some controlled randomness, set by parameters like temperature), adds it to the text, and repeats. ## How are LLMs trained? LLM training usually happens in stages: | **Stage** | **What happens** | **Why it matters** | |---|---|---| | **Pretraining** | The model learns to predict the next token across a huge, broad text corpus. | Builds general language ability and world knowledge. | | **Fine-tuning** | The model is trained further on curated examples, like question-and-answer pairs or instructions. | Teaches it to follow instructions and respond helpfully in conversation. | | **Preference tuning** | Humans or other models rank outputs, and the model is tuned toward preferred responses (for example, RLHF). | Improves helpfulness, tone, and safety. | | **Runtime context** | At inference, the model receives a prompt plus retrieved documents, data, and tool results. | This is where most enterprise customization happens. | Most companies never train an LLM from scratch. LLMs.content: [Partner Content](https://www.weforum.org/partners) # AI can win a maths olympiad but can’t read a clock. Here’s why that matters Published Nov 19, 2026 ![Image 1: Abstract image of neural AI networks](https://assets.weforum.org/cms/images/articles/319103/fd048d579d8f_cropped-0539afc32122-istock-636754212.jpg?w=1024) AI models that can accomplish one task can fail at others due to a phenomenon known as 'jagged intelligence'.Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto NM Nikhil Malhotra Chief Innovation Officer, Tech Mahindra [Centre for AI Excellence](https://centres.weforum.org/centre-for-ai-excellence/) * Large language models may be good at mimicking reasoning, but they struggle to reason through simple causality. Neurosymbolic AI can help solve this conundrum. It may seem counterintuitive to see an artificial intelligence (AI) model solve an International Mathematical Olympiad-level problem with flying colours yet be unable to tell the time accurately on an analogue clock. However, this has indeed happened. Google DeepMind’s Gemini Deep Think was able to score 35 points at the 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad and earn a gold medal, all while thinking in natural language, according to [Stanford’s 2026 AI Index Report](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/technical-performance). The best model of the same generation, tested on visual reasoning AI benchmark ClockBench, read the clock correctly only 50.6% of the time, compared with 90.1% for humans. When the models fail, they tend to be [one to three hours off](https://hai.stanford.edu/assets/files/ai_index_report_2026_chapter_2_technical.pdf), whereas a human would be about three minutes off. One promising answer to addressing this inconsistency is neurosymbolic AI, which pairs the pattern learning of neural networks with the rule-following logic of symbolic systems. ## Why jagged AI is an operational risk Large language models (LLMs) have become extremely good at mimicking reasoning, which is why enterprises are building them into everyday work. They create long chains of thought that help produce good code, concise document summaries and original maths proofs. But what they still struggle to do is reliably identify properties of the world around them or reason through simple causality. AI models that can accomplish one task can fail miserably at others. Researchers call this “[jagged intelligence](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/technical-performance)” –also known as the “jagged frontier” – which highlights the unpredictable [boundary between tasks best suited for humans and those for machines](https://www.weforum.org/stories/emerging-technologies/ai-business-culture-competitive-advantage). This is important, as building workflows around AI that can fail at any given moment creates a vulnerability in an enterprise’s products and operations. Models can also insert hallucinated details into contracts, misunderstand a customer’s issue or create compliance violations. The risk is measurable. In fact, no model scores above 70.2% on [τ-bench](https://hai.stanford.edu/assets/files/ai_index_report_2026_chapter_2_technical.pdf), a benchmark that measures how well AI agents complete real-world tasks using tools while following policy rules. Models are falling short in real-world scenarios as well. On benchmarks from Vals AI, [reported in the AI Index](https://hai.stanford.edu/assets/files/ai_index_report_2026_chapter_2_technical.pdf), the best models achieve only 69.4% accuracy when extracting information from mortgage tax certificates, 68.3% on long financial documents such as credit agreements and 63.3% on entry-level financial analyst tasks. For business leaders, this means AI reliability is an operational risk that needs to be managed, and a model’s standout results offer minimal assurance of how consistently it will perform inside their own workflows. ## Where neurosymbolic AI comes in As its name indicates, neurosymbolic AI merges neural net...

AI Product.titleZh: Anthropic’s IPO shows AI’s value, but enterprises should stay wary | TechTarget
AI Product.content: Anthropic today became the first AI model maker to go public, just a week shy of the fourth anniversary of the launch of its archrival OpenAI’s pioneering ChatGPT, bolstering the value of AI for enterprises that are still struggling with the ROI of the technology and overshadowing AI competitors. The historic public offering from the creator of the Claude line of generative AI models started at $110.50, 34% above the IPO price set on Wednesday. It raised about $81.3 billion across 980 million shares, shattering SpaceX's previous $75 billion record. With the vendor's first day trading on the public market - under the stock ticker symbol ANT - exceeding expectations, it also provided some assurance across the AI industry that financial value lies in the technology, even as enterprises are still scurrying to demonstrate ROI in how they have incorporated it. "The fact they got way above the offering price should give enterprises confidence that enterprise AI is a real thing," said Nick Patience, an analyst at Futurum Group. "For CIOs in some ways it lowers the risk of betting on the company." The dramatic public offering comes after Anthropic initially predicted its valuation would be about $1.33 trillion. The actual value ended up at $1.5 trillion. That initial devaluation in early November followed the Nov. 3 mid-term elections, which revealed widespread negative sentiment in the U.S. about AI and AI data centers. It also comes amid an AI market grappling with the reality of expensive technology that has mostly yet to yield a return. The lack of immediate ROI has led AI vendors, including Anthropic, to try to pacify enterprise concerns by cutting prices. Not only did Anthropic’s first day being listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange give some measure of certainty to enterprises, but it also provided even more visibility to vendor’s technology. ### **What the new funding means** The generative AI startup has spent the six years since it was founded focusing on the enterprise market, compared to OpenAI, which has only lately made serious inroads with businesses. So, the record-breaking IPO suggests that Anthropic’s approach is correct. Its successful debut as a public company means it can now continue to purchase compute and raise debt easily. "Anthropic was already sitting on more than $100 billion before the IPO," Patience noted. "The new money buys it use over its supply chains." He added that Anthropic can now step into some of the deals that before appeared uncertain, using prepayments or guarantees to secure capacity. "Over time, it could own more of its infrastructure outright," Patience continued. The Medical Record Review & Summarization Agent assembles a patient's history with each finding linked to its source document \[1]. The Safety & Incident Investigation Agent surfaces recurring patterns in safety reports rather than processing them in arrival order. The Clinical Documentation & Quality Review Agent drafts reports for clinician sign-off and checks documentation against hospital guidelines \[1]. Open Source AI.content: Member-only story # 9 Free GitHub Repos That Make AI Tools Way More Powerful ## From smarter Claude workflows to better-looking websites and native Mac apps, these open-source projects are worth adding to your AI toolkit. AI tools are getting better, but there's a problem: most people are still using them in exactly the same way. They open Claude, type a prompt, get an answer, and move on. Meanwhile, developers are building entire workflows around AI, using open-source projects that give these tools new capabilities. I went through nine interesting projects that take things a little further. Some help Claude catch mistakes before writing code, others improve website design and SEO, and a few let you build software that would normally require several different tools. Open Source AI.content: # The best things in open source are built together Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion. In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion, more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities. Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine. Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica, an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework. I attended John Maeda and Qianqian Ye’s session at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed. This moment resonated with me. Qianqian asked: *“What do you think the role open-source community plays nowadays in the age of AI?”* John replied: “I worked in the WordPress open source community, where I learned that PHP stands for people helping people. And so if anything, I’m just sort of optimistic that the open source world is the way of how we should do things in general, in society. And I’m really excited how, at GitHub, we care so deeply about open source.” ## Replica, a new open-source design harness In 2025, 60% of the top growing open source projects were AI focused. At GitHub, it is no different. A few weeks ago, GitHub’s design team introduced Replica, which considers the role of designers in the era of AI and focuses on reinforcement learning. Replica started as an internal project, but it proved to be so useful that our design team shared the tool so developers and designers everywhere could also benefit. > GitHub Replica does a lot of reinforcement learning. It’s an open source design harness to enable you to do the kind of things you hope to do in prototyping playground > > John Maeda With Replica, anyone can create AI-generated prototypes within their design system and refine them side-by-side with GitHub Copilot. You can also publish prototypes to a Replica Hub to collaborate with teammates, receive comments, and iterate. With reinforcement learning top of mind, the system learns what good looks like from each interaction and from the comments on the prototypes; it gets better over time. Because Replica is open source, you can hack it and adapt it to fit your teams’ products and workflows however you see fit. ## A11y Framework, a new open-source accessibility framework Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the last year, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. AI has helped us all build faster. With this volume, and more to be expected, we must keep accessibility top of mind so that the code that is being shipped is accessible to all. > As the home for all developers, we want every developer to feel welcome and to be able to contribute to the future of global software development using everything GitHub ha...

Infra & Chips.content: ### AI inference servers shrink to fit the air-cooled racks enterprises already run Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own. As AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead. That gap is opening room for challengers to the incumbent chipmakers. Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera. “Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija said. “We are enabling them now to own it. It’s not that we are helping the world save power or save money — which we are — but it’s that we are unlocking use cases that were simply not possible before.” Botija spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how power-efficient inference chips are heading for the data center and how enterprises locked out by the cost and power of GPU racks can own their own AI infrastructure instead of renting compute. *(* Disclosure below.)* ### Power-efficient inference chips head for the data center Axelera’s Europa chip has been shipping since September. Ahead of SC26, the company unveiled Titania, a third-generation architecture that scales the design up to a 400-watt chip. The resulting six-kilowatt server is built to perform like leading data center GPUs while fitting into the existing 20- to 30-kilowatt air-cooled racks of an ordinary enterprise data center, Botija explained. “Having a six-kilowatt server that can perform like a data centre GPU is a pretty big deal,” he said. “It basically means that they have some storage equipment, some networking equipment, some traditional CPU equipment, and next to all of that, they can also insert some AI inference hardware acceleration without needing to go and rebuild another server room or another data center.” For enterprises that would rather own their AI hardware than pay a recurring cloud bill, the barriers have been steep. A GPU rack costs at least $1 million, often far more, and usually requires liquid cooling, Botija noted. Axelera’s answer rests on digital in-memory computing, a technique that grew out of its founders’ research and gives the company’s power-efficient inference chips a performance-per-watt advantage. “Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija said. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your opex, and therefore be more profitable as a company.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of SC26: *(* Disclosure: NYSE Wired sponsored this segment of theCUBE. Infra & Chips.title: 800 VDC and NVIDIA DSX: the AI factory is changing. Europe's real test is delivery.
Infra & Chips.titleZh: 800 VDC and NVIDIA DSX: the AI factory is changing. Europe's real test is delivery.
Infra & Chips.content: # 800 VDC and NVIDIA DSX: the AI factory is changing. Europe's real test is delivery. The 800 VDC architecture, the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture, and the new NVIDIA 800 VDC roadmap suggest a totally new approach to the implementation of AI infrastructure. In the case of Europe, the question goes beyond technology and is about access to the grid, investment decisions, and a capacity to realize the development opportunity. ## The next generation of AI infrastructure is taking shape Until now, a megawatt of power was a considerable amount in an entire data hall, but NVIDIA is now developing a system whereby a single rack can approach that level of consumption. The consequences for the mechanical and electrical systems are considerable, as well as for the economics of large-scale artificial intelligence. May 2025 saw the presentation of NVIDIA's roadmap for 800VDC, a significant deviation from the conventional data center electrical architecture. Eighteen months later, the transition is moving away from mere paper engineering. The components required are being developed, the reference architectures are becoming increasingly precise, and the first reported commercial deployments are emerging. The pace at which the market is changing has been illustrated by two recent developments. In March NVIDIA launched its DSX AI factory design, then in October it launched the expanded DSX platform and the DSX POD reference architecture. And then on 2 November, China's Envision announced what it described as the first commercial implementation of an integrated 800V power system in a large-scale AI data center. These developments, as individuals, are all technologically important. However, they are pointing to a much deeper change in the way AI infrastructure is going to be designed, built and operated. For years now, data centers have been built with one basic assumption: they provide a reliable power supply, a high-quality building, and enough computing equipment to deliver what the client has paid for. The coming generation of AI-based platforms are putting this assumption to the test. Everything, the computing equipment, power distribution, cooling, power storage, and even interfacing with the local power grid, has become increasingly integrated. As one who has spent much of my career at the intersection of technology, strategy, and data center design, I can tell you that this transition needs a lot more attention from both industry and investors. It is not only a question of increasing the power to the racks, which grow more and more demanding, but of reconsidering the conversion of power into useful work, the financing of the infrastructure, and the execution of projects in markets where the availability of energy is one of the most important restrictions on growth. ## Why 800 VDC is becoming an architectural necessity The rationale behind 800 VDC begins with a relatively simple engineering challenge: AI computing systems are consuming substantially more electricity within increasingly concentrated physical footprints. Traditional enterprise racks commonly operated at between 5 and 10 kW. High-density AI systems now exceed 100 kW, with future architectures targeting several hundred kilowatts per rack, and NVIDIA's Kyber roadmap extends that trajectory toward rack power requirements approaching 1 MW. When you get to that density, you are running up against the limitations of conventional distribution. Electric power is the product of voltage and current, and when you're dealing with relatively low voltage, you need a higher current. That means you need bigger wires, and more losses, and a greater demand on the wiring and electrical system. Infra & Chips.content: # Chinese tech firms fear AI hits from US curbs after Nvidia fallout Chinese tech firms are facing challenges as the U.S. tightens restrictions on access to advanced chips HONG KONG -- Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the U.S. tightens restrictions on China's access to the world's cutting-edge chips. Chinese tech giant Alibaba, which on Thursday announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new U.S. rules could affect some of its global data center expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions. The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centers in third countries, the latest U.S. move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models. Alibaba's AI revenues are surging as demand grows As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing U.S. export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips. But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the U.S. to close what some policymakers called a loophole. As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data center investment plans in China and abroad. Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies. For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53% year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan ($9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10% from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan ($41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected. While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60% during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan ($7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout. Tencent says US chip curb ‘sets everyone back in China’ Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new U.S. rule on chip access “sets everyone back in China.” “Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said. “Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new U.S. rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute. A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centers could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster. Infra & Chips.title: Nvidia Faces a New China Reality After Trump's Latest AI Chip Comments
Infra & Chips.titleZh: Nvidia Faces a New China Reality After Trump's Latest AI Chip Comments
Infra & Chips.content: This article first appeared on GuruFocus. President Donald Trump indicated that Nvidia (NVDA, Financials) may be allowed to sell its Blackwell AI chips to China at some point, because they would become obsolete with newer processors.Exports of Blackwell might be palatable in two or three years as chip technology improves, Trump told Fox News in an interview at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China.The statements suggest U.S. export limits might be eased in the future but the U.S. government did not announce any immediate changes in policy.Nvidia no longer ships its most powerful AI processors to China, despite a license deal between Washington and Beijing.Interim CEO Colette Kress stated on Tuesday's results conference that there are no plans for any more shipments for now.The company said it had $2.4 billion in sales of licensed Hopper-generation data center systems to China in the quarter ended Oct. 25.The chipmaker's quarterly sales grew 103% year over year to $115.8 billion, driven by sustained demand for Blackwell processors and the fast growth of its Vera Rubin platform.China is still a big prospective market for high-end semiconductor devices, but export controls hinder Nvidia's access.Trump's comments imply that older-generation chips may ultimately be permitted for export once new devices join the market.Investors will look for changes in U.S. export policy and the company's future forecast on China sales to determine possible revenue effect.
